summary: Proposes mechanisms that let Realm Specific IP work with end-to-end IPsec. Because IPsec protects packets in ways that address translation tends to break, the memo describes how an RSIP host can still use it. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A sealed letter breaks if someone rewrites the address on the envelope. This explains how to get a proper address first so the seal stays safe.

questions: how does rsip work with ipsec
how does address translation break encryption
can you use rsip and ipsec together
subtitle: Making end-to-end IPsec work through address translation

tldr.problem: When an RSIP server translates addresses to make private hosts appear public, encrypted security connections (IPsec) break because the encryption protects the IP address fields themselves.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds RSIP extensions to coordinate address and security keys between the private host, the RSIP server, and the remote peer, using unique identifiers (Initiator Cookies for IKE negotiation, SPIs for encrypted flows) instead of relying on IP addresses to distinguish connections.
tldr.outcome: Multiple private hosts can share one public address and use IPsec with external servers, but only if both the IPsec implementation and the RSIP server are aware of each other. This protocol remains experimental.

today: RFC 3104 is classified as Experimental. It proposes extensions to RSIP that would allow RSIP clients to use end-to-end IPsec, but since RSIP itself has not been widely deployed, these extensions remain largely theoretical. The RFC notes significant operational complexities and limitations, and the IESG cautions that the costs and benefits of using RSIP should be carefully weighed against other solutions to address shortage.

sections.title: The Problem: IPsec and Address Translation
sections.content:
RSIP (Realm Specific IP) is a technique where a server translates addresses, allowing many private hosts to share one public address. IPsec is a standard way to encrypt and authenticate IP packets. The conflict: IPsec encrypts the entire packet, including the IP address headers. When an RSIP server changes the source address, the encryption breaks because the packet no longer matches the signature that protects it.

This RFC specifies how to make them work together. The solution requires both the IPsec implementation and the RSIP server to cooperate, using unique identifiers instead of IP addresses to tell connections apart.
sections.eli5: A secret code proves a letter came from a real sender and wasn't opened. If we change the address on the envelope after the code is made, the code becomes invalid. The trick is to create the code before changing the address.

sections.title: The RSIP-IPsec Model
sections.content:
The architecture has three parts: a private host X (the RSIP client), a gateway N (the RSIP server) with addresses in both the private and public network, and a remote host Y on the public network.

Host X sends IPsec packets destined for Y through its local RSIP server N, which translates them to appear as if they come from N's public address. Y sends encrypted packets back to N's public address. The challenge is that N and X must agree on unique identifiers for each flow so that N can route incoming encrypted packets back to the right private host, and Y must know which client on the other side of N it is actually talking to.

The RFC assumes the RSIP-IP variant and proposes using two mechanisms: for IKE (the key exchange protocol), use the Initiator Cookie field; for IPsec data flows, use the SPI (Security Parameter Index).
sections.eli5: Imagine a mail distribution center where many people share one mailbox. The center marks each sealed letter with a secret code so it knows who it belongs to when it arrives back.

sections.title: Handling the Key Exchange (IKE)
sections.content:
IKE (Internet Key Exchange) is the protocol that two peers use to agree on encryption keys before they can exchange IPsec packets. Normally IKE uses port 500. When an RSIP client X wants to negotiate keys with a remote host Y, it sends IKE packets through the RSIP server N.

The problem: N needs to match incoming IKE responses from Y back to the correct client X. If X uses port 500 (the standard), N cannot use ports to distinguish between X and other clients on the same public address. Instead, the RFC specifies using the Initiator Cookie field in the IKE header, a 64-bit value that X and N negotiate. N uses this cookie to demultiplex incoming responses and route them back to X. The RFC allows a simple trial-and-error approach: X picks a random cookie, and if N detects a collision with an existing flow, X retries. Given the 64-bit space, collisions are extremely rare.
sections.eli5: Two people in the same building phone a friend to arrange a meeting. Instead of saying their own names, they use a secret code they made up. When the friend calls back, they use the same secret code so the receptionist knows which person to patch through.

sections.title: Protecting the Data (IPsec Flows)
sections.content:
Once keys are negotiated, IPsec uses the SPI (Security Parameter Index) as a label for each encrypted flow. X and N must agree on which SPI values to use, and they must be unique both at X (the client side) and at N (the gateway side).

X requests an SPI from N via an ASSIGN_REQUEST_RSIPSEC message. N can assign one if requested, or X can suggest one. Once assigned, N uses the SPI to demultiplex incoming IPsec packets: the triple of (IPsec protocol number, SPI, and destination IP address) uniquely identifies a flow at N. When N receives an IPsec packet matching one of these tuples, it tunnels it to the correct private client X. The RFC defines new RSIP message types and an SPI parameter to carry this information.
sections.eli5: Each sealed letter gets a unique tracking number. When it arrives at the mail center, the number tells the worker which mailbox it belongs to.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
Several important constraints apply. First, the remote host Y must not rely on IP address alone to identify which client it is talking to. Instead, Y's security policy must use session-oriented or user-oriented identification (the IKE Identification Payload). This is necessary because multiple RSIP clients may use the same public address.

Second, IPsec bump-in-the-stack (BITS) implementations that intercept packets at the OS level cannot work out of the box with RSIP, because they need to coordinate SPI assignments with the RSIP server. Standard IPsec stacks that are aware of RSIP can do this coordination.

Third, the RFC cautions that SPIs normally carry entropy to defend against denial-of-service attacks; requiring them to be negotiated and unique reduces this entropy slightly. However, the negotiation itself adds security by requiring the RSIP server to verify SPI uniqueness before allowing use.
sections.eli5: The system only works if everyone plays by the rules: the mail center must tell the friend whose letter just arrived which building it came from (not just the mailbox number), and the building's internal system has to understand what the mail center is doing.

sections.title: Security Impact
sections.content:
The RFC argues this approach is more secure than traditional NAT. Traditional NAT arbitrarily rewrites addresses without coordination, which breaks IPsec. RSIP with this extension adds a negotiation phase where the RSIP server and client explicitly agree on identifiers, giving both parties control over the mapping.

However, unlike address-based security policies, this approach requires the endpoints to use more sophisticated identification methods. If a remote host Y relies only on seeing the same source IP address for every packet, the method fails. The security relies on assuming Y uses proper cryptographic identification through IKE.

One security point: SPI values should be semi-random to serve as anti-clogging tokens against spoofed attack packets. Negotiating SPIs slightly reduces entropy, but this is a minor trade-off for enabling IPsec through address translation.
sections.eli5: Making someone negotiate with you before changing their address is safer than secretly changing it. But it only works if they trust that the person they are negotiating with is really who they say they are.
